newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines pilots reject key labor contract.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines pilots reject key labor contract.

text.p: American Airlines pilots Wednesday rejected a new four-year labour contract, dealing a heavy blow to the carrier's plans to keep down costs and overhaul its fleet.
More than 60 percent of Allied Pilots Association members voted against the labour pact, which would have given them a 3 percent wage increase this year and an additional 2 percent in 1999.

American Airlines, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., said it was "extremely disappointed" by the rejection but did not say whether or not it would eventually scuttle ambitious plans to overhaul its fleet.
The airline last November pledged to buy 103 jets from Boeing Co. and take out options on 527 more in one of the biggest commercial airplane orders in history.

But Chief Executive Officer Robert Crandall insisted then that the Boeing deal, which at list prices was worth about $6.5 billion and potentially as much as $35 billion, would only go through if pilots ratified the new labour contract.
Airline officials said Wednesday's vote effectively put the Boeing deal on hold but did not automatically mean it would be scrapped.
"We did say it would be contingent on a pilot deal and we'll need to continue looking at that. We obviously don't have a deal yet," spokeswoman Andrea Rader said.
"It's a shock," said Boeing spokeswoman Liz Verdier. But she said Boeing was confident the airline would resolve its differences with the pilots.

"We have a 20-year relationship with American set up," Verdier said. "This is one of those glitches in a relationship." Airplane deliveries to American under the sales agreement are not scheduled to begin until mid-1998.
Industry analysts said the surprise rejection of the contract put American's modest long-term growth plans in question.

"It is going to have a definite impact on its stock," said James Higgins, an analyst with Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette. "I don't know if the pilots fully appreciate what they are playing with... They risk the company just saying that the economics don't justify continuing our investment plans."
The carrier said in a statement that it was consulting with the pilots association board of directors and mediators on the future of the contract negotiations.
A tentative agreement was thrashed out last September after two years of tortuous negotiations. The union's board backed the contract, but rank-and-file members voted against it.
"The membership has had its say, and we'll have to roll up our sleeves and get busy," union spokesman Gregg Overman said, adding that union leaders would meet Thursday to discuss their next step.
He said 5,046 members voted against the proposed contract and only 3,197 voted in favour. More than 95 percent of the 8,600 union members eligible to vote did so.
American Airlines said the National Mediation Board, which brokered the tentative agreement, could declare an impasse in the negotiations and offer binding arbitration to both sides.
The carrier said that if either party then rejected arbitration, a 30-day cooling-off period would begin.

"If there is no agreement by the conclusion of this period, the union would be free to strike, and the airline would be free to implement new pay and work rules it bargained over during the negotiations," the airline said in a statement.

Many pilots had wanted bigger wage increases and bitterly opposed a clause allowing the airline to buy regional jets for its commuter carrier American Eagle, which currently operates only turboprop aircraft.
In return, American was forced to drop its plans to set up a low-fare short-haul unit in which pilots would have taken a pay cut of up to 30 percent.

From the beginning, the tentative agreement was seen by Wall Street as giving the airline some productivity gains but most analysts said it did not eliminate American's cost disadvantages vis-a-vis its competitors or provide it with major incentives to expand.
When American Airlines and Boeing unveiled their blockbuster deal in November, Crandall said it represented more a modernisation than a rapid expansion of its fleet.
